description: Nodara Tech is a Costa Rican team combining software, UX/UI, and financial strategy. We seek collaborators interested in game design, astronomy, space exploration, science education, and storytelling to build engaging, accessible solutions.
summary:
We developed a tool for exploring historical hotspot detections from the MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors in a harmonized database.

We analyzed user profiles and needs to guide the tool’s design. We compared two spatial harmonization methods, the H3 hexagonal grid and a regular grid, to organize detections from both sensors into common spatial units and make them easier to compare over time.

The tool preserves the historical record of satellite detections, makes it easier to compare data across sensors, and supports more consistent monitoring of hotspots that may indicate active fires.
details:
FIRETRACE HARMONIZATION is a web application to explore and compare thermal activity detections obtained by MODIS and VIIRS satellites, based on NASA FIRMS records. It allows selecting a region and a period, consulting a detection map, and observing their evolution through statistics, a daily chart, and an intensity calendar. The colors of the points help distinguish levels of Fire Radiative Power (FRP), without interpreting each point as an individual fire.

Its engine normalizes the records of each sensor and groups them spatially using two methods: a square cell grid and the H3 hexagonal index. Additionally, it identifies possible matches between observations close in space and time. Time windows and quality filters allow evaluating how those matches change according to the chosen parameters. The system preserves the provenance of the records to avoid confusing data combination with a proven physical equivalence.

It brings together information from two satellite technologies in an accessible interface and facilitates analyzing regions with different characteristics without manually handling multiple CSV files. It allows identifying periods of higher activity, contrasting patterns between sensors, exploring possible shared areas, and exporting results. It also provides transparency: groupings, matching windows, and confidence filters can be compared instead of being presented as invisible decisions to the user.

 

The project seeks to facilitate the study of spatial and temporal patterns of thermal activity and support the communication of satellite information to students, researchers, and teams interested in fire management. It can serve as a basis for broader historical analyses and for exploring methods of integrating observations from different sensors. In its current state, it is an exploratory analysis prototype, not a certified early warning system nor a tool that determines with certainty the amount of real fires.

 

The processing, normalization, matching, and query logic was developed primarily in Python. The web interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Leaflet to visualize maps and geographical points. H3-py was used for hexagonal indexing and PyShp to work with territorial boundaries. Records come from NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS); the cartographic background uses map and satellite imagery services such as Esri, with the corresponding attribution. Visual Studio Code and web browsers were used for programming and testing. The prototype runs via a local server and does not require proprietary satellite hardware: a conventional computer, Python, and an Internet connection to load certain map layers are sufficient.

 

Its contribution is not limited to showing points on a map. It integrates two satellite resolutions with different spatial methods — grid and H3 — and distinguishes a match on the same day from a candidate correspondence between close passes. Furthermore, it incorporates five audits aimed at explaining the results: temporal concordance, sensitivity to different time windows, proper matching in H3, the effect of cell area and borders, and the effect of confidence filters. This combination of technical analysis and visualization allows studying both patterns and the limitations of their interpretation.

 

We considered the resolution difference between MODIS and VIIRS, observation times, the approximate location of pixel centers, and the distinct confidence scales of each sensor. We also evaluated the risk of counting repeated observations as different fires, cell border effects, the sensitivity of matches to filters, and interface performance when visualizing many records. Therefore, the map may display a sample to maintain fluidity, while statistics use the records of the selected period.

We prioritized a reproducible, easy-to-use, and scientifically defensible prototype within the available time. The tool shows detected activity and candidate matches; it does not interpret those indicators as confirmed fire probabilities. Validation with independent observations and a fully calibrated historical series between sensors are identified as future steps.

Processed data from Costa Rica and Afghanistan, with tools to query or process United States states depending on the information available in the installation.

Complete 2000–2026 coverage is not claimed.
